Stress placement on polymorphemic words (i.e. verbs and possessed nouns) is grammatically conditioned ... For monomorphemic words stress, [+stress], falls on the first closed syllable (which is usually though not necessarily the last syllable in the word) or, if there is no closed syllable, then on the first syllable. sweep_summary: All three stress-keyword titles attached to amel1241 in Glottolog (Nedergaard Thomsen 1992 on Danish unit accentuation, Buiten & compilation 1965 on an L2 prosody-training device, Touster 1955 on Beowulf metrics) are mis-attachments sharing only the word 'device'; none concerns Amele, none was downloaded, all priority none (Crossref records and logged). No new Amele stress source surfaced. I re-read the held primary, Roberts 1986 UCL thesis pp. 364-365 (text + page scan at and Roberts 2016 pp. 76-77 and 422-423: the catalog quote is verbatim at the cited place, the classification (weight-sensitive, rightmost closed syllable else initial, word-final off-glide counts as closed, no stress levels, domain = monomorphemic words) is confirmed, and the 2016 rule (12.59) 'read the word from right to left' fixes the right edge. Nothing supersedes the catalog's deciding source. The UCL Discovery record page now could not be reached by automated download

new_statements.quote: There is no distinction between different levels of stress. ... There are two patterns of stress placement depending on the morphological structure of the word. Stress placement on monomorphemic words (i.e. all words except verbs and possessed nouns) is phonologically conditioned and predictable. ... For monomorphemic words stress, [+stress], falls on the first closed syllable (which is usually though not necessarily the last syllable in the word) or, if there is no closed syllable, then on the first syllable. For the purposes of stress placement an off-glide functions as a closed syllable when it occurs in word final position. In other word positions it functions as an open syllable.

new_statements.locator: Roberts 1986, sections 3.3.2.3 'Distinctions between different levels of stress' and 3.3.2.4-5 'Position of stress', printed pp. 364-365 (PDF pages 364-365; page scan, in the same folder; text). Confirmed against Roberts 2016 pp. 76-77 and pp. 422-423.
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, unbounded, no secondary stress: in monomorphemic words (everything except verbs and possessed nouns) stress the closed syllable nearest the word end (word-final off-glide counts as closed; word-internal off-glides do not), else the initial syllable. Roberts 2016 makes the direction explicit ('first closed syllable nearest to the end of the word'; rule 12.59b 'read the word from right to left'; [duʔ.dʊ.ˈʔul] 'horizon', [ʒæ.ˈwæl.ti] 'wind from north', [ˈæn.se] 'left hand', [ˈnu.i] 'island'). Verbs and possessed nouns take grammatically conditioned stress. This confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and its rightmost-closed-syllable reading against StressTyp2's leftmost-heavy reading.

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, unbounded, rightmost closed syllable else initial; word-final off-glide counts as closed; no secondary stress; domain = monomorphemic words) rests on the full reference grammar by the language's principal describer (Roberts 1986 UCL thesis = 1987 Croom Helm) and his 2016 433-page RRG grammatical sketch, both held with text layers and page scan, and the deciding quotations are verbatim at the cited places (1986:364-365 exact; 2016 printed pages are 76-77 and 422-423 rather than 76/421-422, a footer-pagination slip with identical content). The 2016 formalisation ('nearest to the end of the word', 'read the word from right to left', [duʔ.dʊ.ˈʔul] 'horizon' HLH stressed on 3) settles the edge against StressTyp2/Hayes's leftmost reading, and the compilers scan of ~100 stress-marked monomorphemic forms found one departure ([ˈdæɛʔ] 'cold'). No phonology article
